## The iterative workflow

We use the iterative Bayesian workflow described by @gelmanBayesianWorkflow2020: specify a transparent model, simulate from its priors, fit it, inspect computation and predictive behaviour, identify a concrete inadequacy, and only then add complexity. The numbered models preserve that development history. A later number is not automatically better; an extension must solve a named problem and survive the same checks as its predecessor. The model inventory records which models are development steps, references, or candidates for substantive reporting.

## Fitting pipeline and sampling configurations

Models are defined in PyMC and sampled with NUTS through nutpie. Every registered model follows the same ordered pipeline: prepare data; construct priors and hyperparameters; build the probability model; run prior predictive checks; sample the posterior; calculate diagnostics; run posterior predictive checks; summarise the posterior; produce plots; and prepare the model report. The `dev` configuration uses short chains for quick code development, `test` supports stronger integration checks, and `rep` produces reporting-quality fits. Development and test output may be useful for debugging but cannot source numerical claims in this report.

Each fit is first written to an isolated staging directory. A machine-readable state file records whether it is initialising, running, complete, or failed. Only after the statistical pipeline succeeds is the staged directory atomically promoted to the canonical model-output location. Quarto rendering then runs against that promoted fit as a separate, retryable step: a rendering failure cannot discard a completed multi-hour fit. If the statistical pipeline fails, the preceding complete fit remains in place and the failed staging output is retained separately for diagnosis.

## Validation checks

Every model in this report is held to the same checks; the per-model evidence is in Appendix B.

### Prior predictive checks

Before observing the study outcomes, we draw trajectories and replicated vocabulary scores from the prior model. We require bounded scores, plausible levels at the youngest and oldest relevant ages, developmental changes that are smooth on a realistic time scale, and enough dispersion to represent heterogeneous children without assigning substantial probability to implausible extremes. A prior predictive failure is addressed by revising the scientific assumptions or their parameterisation, not by inspecting the posterior and quietly selecting a prior that reproduces the fitted result.

### Convergence diagnostics {#sec-convergence}

Every reported fit is screened against four diagnostics, applied uniformly across all models and in **two tiers**.

The **hard tier** is fail-closed: a potential scale reduction factor $\hat{R} \le 1.01$ and bulk and tail effective sample size (ESS) $\ge 400$ on every sampled parameter. A fit that misses either does not proceed — posterior summaries, report generation, rendering and upload do not run — because a chain that has not mixed cannot be summarised at all. The ESS floor is the per-chain recommendation of @vehtariRankNormalizationFolding2021 — at least 100 effective draws per chain, hence 400 across the four chains we run — below which the $\hat{R}$ and ESS estimators are themselves too noisy to trust; it is a reliability floor for the diagnostics, not a guarantee that every summary is settled to its last digit. The hard tier is screened element-wise, so vector-valued parameters (the GP basis coefficients and, where present, the study- and subject-level random intercepts) are held to the same thresholds as the scalars.

The **soft tier** is recorded rather than fail-closed: no divergent transitions, and an energy Bayesian fraction of missing information (BFMI) $\ge 0.3$ on every chain. Both bear on how far into the posterior's tails the sampler reached, so they qualify the interval bounds more than the point estimates. A fit that clears the hard tier but not the soft tier remains reportable — for several models in this family a handful of divergences, or a BFMI slightly below 0.3, has not been removable by longer tuning without an infeasible reparameterisation — but it is marked, and it cannot be syndicated into this report as a clean fit without that mark being carried with it. Each model's appendix entry carries a generated banner recording all four diagnostics against their achieved values (@sec-appendix-b1), so a soft-tier caveat is visible wherever that model's numbers are read.

Where a development-configuration fit misses the hard tier — short chains routinely miss the ESS target — its estimates are treated as provisional until refitted at reporting quality.

Bulk and tail ESS are both gated because they govern different summaries: bulk-ESS bounds the Monte-Carlo error of the central summaries (the mean and median we tabulate), while tail-ESS bounds the error of the quantiles that form the credible intervals we lead with (@sec-interval-convention). Each fit's diagnostics table records the achieved bulk-ESS, tail-ESS, $\hat{R}$ and Monte-Carlo standard error (MCSE) for every sampled parameter, so each can be judged on its own mixing rather than on a single pass/fail line; the 400-draw floor corresponds to an MCSE of about $\text{SD}/\sqrt{400} \approx 5\%$ of a parameter's posterior standard deviation for a central summary, enough to fix the few significant figures we report. Post-hoc derived quantities — the GP mean function over the age grid, expected counts, milestone ages — are smooth functions of those sampled parameters and inherit their mixing rather than being gated separately; because a derived quantity can in principle mix worse than any single parent, we treat its tail summaries with the same caution and, for the skewed short-list below, do not read them to their last digit.

### Posterior predictive checks

Posterior predictive checks generate replicated outcomes from each fitted model and compare them with the observations. We inspect probability-mass and cumulative-distribution overlays, the distribution of bounded counts across age, and age-specific summaries. For joint models we check understood and produced outcomes together, including violations and fallback rows in the nested likelihood. The signing model additionally checks the four sign-by-speech cells used to identify their association. A model can pass sampler diagnostics yet fail these checks: convergence shows that computation characterised the specified posterior, not that the specification adequately represents the data.

### Quantitative predictive calibration {#sec-predictive-calibration}

The overlays above are read by eye. Every fit additionally writes a numerical calibration table, so the same question is answered in numbers that can be compared across models, outcomes and ages. For each outcome it records, pooled overall and within 12-month age bands: the mean observed and predicted counts and their difference; the **empirical coverage** of the predictive interval at each reported width; and the distribution of the **probability integral transform** (PIT) — the position of each observation within its own predictive distribution, summarised by its mean, its variance, and the proportion falling in the extreme 5% tails. Because the outcomes are discrete counts, the mid-PIT is used, which assigns half the replicated mass equal to the observation.

A well-calibrated model has coverage near nominal, a PIT mean near 0.5, and a PIT variance near $1/12 \approx 0.083$, the variance of a standard uniform. Departures are directional: PIT variance *below* that value with coverage *above* nominal means the predictive distribution is wider than the data warrant; PIT variance above it with coverage below nominal means the model is overconfident. A PIT mean away from 0.5 indicates systematic bias, and an inflated extreme rate indicates observations the model treats as near-impossible.

Two limits on how far these numbers can be pushed. First, they are **in-sample**: the replications condition on parameters that the same observations informed, so the PIT is expected to be somewhat under-dispersed and coverage somewhat above nominal even for a well-specified model. The direction of a departure is therefore not by itself evidence that the reported intervals are conservative for a *new* child; the out-of-sample counterpart is the LOO/ELPD comparison in @sec-supersedes. Their value is in comparison — between models, between outcomes, and across age — and in catching gross misfit, which is where an interval-coverage failure would first appear. Second, pooling over ages can conceal an age-specific failure, which is why each model's own report carries the age-banded breakdown; bands holding a handful of observations are uninformative by construction.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-calibration-cross-model
#| tbl-cap: "Posterior-predictive calibration of each model of record, pooled over ages. Nominal is the outer predictive width each fit tabulated. PIT variance is compared against 1/12 = 0.083."
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd

from vocab_growth.models.calibration import overall_calibration
from vocab_growth.models.definitions import MODEL_REGISTRY

_rows = []
for _model in MODEL_REGISTRY.values():
    _table = load_summary(_model.model_id, "posterior_predictive_calibration")
    if _table is None or _table.empty:
        continue
    _overall, _level = overall_calibration(_table)
    for _, _row in _overall.iterrows():
        _rows.append(
            {
                "Model": _model.model_id,
                "Outcome": _row["outcome"],
                "n": int(_row["n_observations"]),
                "Nominal": f"{_level:.0%}",
                "Coverage": round(float(_row["empirical_coverage"]), 3),
                "Mean error": round(float(_row["mean_error"]), 1),
                "PIT mean": round(float(_row["mid_pit_mean"]), 3),
                "PIT variance": round(float(_row["mid_pit_variance"]), 3),
                "PIT extreme rate": round(float(_row["mid_pit_extreme_rate"]), 3),
            }
        )

show_or_pending(
    pd.DataFrame(_rows) if _rows else None,
    "the per-model posterior-predictive calibration tables",
)
```

### Reporting estimates: lead with the interval

Several estimands in this report rest on modest samples — most acutely the sign–speech association $\psi$, identified from roughly 34 children. At that precision a point estimate selected because it looks "significant" (for example, because its interval excludes a reference value) is on average inflated in magnitude, and at low power can even take the wrong sign — the Type-M and Type-S errors that follow from selecting on a noisy estimate (the "winner's curse"). We therefore lead with the credible interval and the strength of evidence for a named claim, and treat the point estimate as the least informative summary rather than the headline.

### The reported interval: median, 50% and 89% {#sec-interval-convention}

For every parameter and derived quantity we report the posterior **median**, an inner **50%** and an outer **89%** credible interval, and — through the density and posterior-predictive plots — the **full posterior distribution** rather than an interval alone [@kruschkeBayesianAnalysisReporting2021]. Intervals are **equal-tailed** (percentile-based) by default; a small, named set of strongly skewed or boundary-censored estimands — the sign–speech association $\psi$, the Beta-Binomial concentration $\kappa$, and milestone/peak ages — is instead reported with **highest-density intervals**, where an equal-tailed interval would misrepresent the credible region. Each table and figure states which kind it uses.

The width is **89%**, not the more familiar 95%. The choice is deliberate. A conventional interval width carries no special epistemic status — 95% is inherited from frequentist testing, and the essential requirement is only that whatever width is used be reported clearly [@kruschkeBayesianAnalysisReporting2021] — and treating any width as a threshold invites reading an interval as a hypothesis test. A non-round width discourages that reading [@mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020]. It is also more stable to estimate from MCMC. The tail-ESS reported for every parameter is defined at the 5% and 95% quantiles — it is calibrated to a 90% interval — so it certifies the 5.5th and 94.5th percentiles of an 89% equal-tailed interval almost exactly, whereas for a 95% interval the same diagnostic understates the difficulty of its more extreme 2.5th and 97.5th limits. An equal-tailed 89% interval is therefore both better-diagnosed and more reproducible at a given effective sample size than a 95% one. This is a *relative* advantage, not a claim that the 400-draw gate settles every limit: the order-of-10,000 effective draws Kruschke associates with stable interval limits are calibrated to 95% highest-density intervals [@kruschkeBayesianAnalysisReporting2021], and an 89% width needs somewhat fewer (of order 6,000 on normal-theory scaling) — still far more than the reliability floor. Highest-density limits on a skewed posterior are the most demanding case: one limit sits further into a tail, and unlike an equal-tailed interval the HDI is not transformation-invariant. The small HDI short-list ($\psi$, $\kappa$, boundary-censored ages) is therefore read with the Type-M/Type-S caution above rather than to its last reported digit. Because we report the full posterior, a reader who prefers another width can read it off directly.

### What the reported intervals include

The uncertainty bands in this report are of two kinds, and their scope differs. **Population-trajectory intervals** — the expected-count intervals and the milestone-age summaries — are posterior uncertainty on the **zero-effect** trajectory — the *typical* (median) child in the average study, since the random effects are symmetric around zero on the logit scale and the inverse-logit is monotone, which is not the arithmetic average of children's counts. They narrow as data accrue and do not describe how far individual children spread around that curve. **New-child predictive intervals**, where reported (the bivariate random-effect models), additionally draw a fresh child from the estimated subject-level variance, but hold the study random effect at zero — so they describe a new child *in an average study* and omit the between-study heterogeneity a genuinely new cohort would carry. Two consequences follow. The joint sign/speech model (VG15) currently reports only population-level expected-count uncertainty and has no new-child predictive-count intervals at all. And the milestone tables (`time_to_milestone`) report the posterior interval on the *population* trajectory's milestone age — the age at which the zero-effect trajectory reaches a target — not a spread across slow, typical and fast children; a "fast child" milestone would require the full new-child predictive draws. Widening these to full new-cohort predictive intervals (subject *and* study variance, plus VG15 predictive counts) is a noted refinement, not yet built.

## Model comparison and what "supersedes" means {#sec-supersedes}

A later model is said to **supersede** an earlier one only on two combined grounds, reported together:

1. **Tabulated out-of-sample comparison** — LOO / expected log pointwise predictive density (ELPD), reported as a comparison table with standard errors of the difference, so the improvement is quantified rather than asserted.
2. **Identified structural issue** — a concrete, named modelling problem in the earlier model that the later one resolves (e.g. study composition confounding a population curve; a GP↔intercept identifiability ridge; an independence assumption that is not data-identified).

The status taxonomy is: **model of record**, the current source for a stated estimand; **development step**, retained to show how structure was added but not preferred for headline estimates; **TD reference**, a typically-developing comparison model with a distinct population role; and **superseded**, replaced after a documented structural or data problem. A superseded model never supplies a number in the findings. The inventory in Appendix A is the source of truth for these roles; lineage-specific comparison tables report the relevant ELPD evidence rather than collapsing models with different populations or outcomes into one inappropriate ranking.

## Provenance and reproducibility

Every fit carries a generated manifest containing the complete registered model definition, sampling configuration and parameters, prepared-data fingerprint and source counts, raw-input fingerprint, Git commit and dirty state, Python and operating-system details, and installed package versions. Resume checks require the requested sampling tier, model definition, raw data, and Git revision to match; the existence of `trace.nc` is not sufficient. Sampling checks compare statistical effort rather than machine layout: draws, tuning iterations, chains and target acceptance must meet or exceed the named tier, while the host-dependent number of parallel cores is ignored. This permits a documented higher-tuning refit without accepting a weaker fit. Figure synchronisation and upload additionally require an explicitly complete, convergence-passing, reporting-quality fit with a rendered report and clean recorded source state. A later documentation-only commit does not invalidate that fit for publication, because the fit's own revision remains recorded in its manifest. Quarto's `freeze: true` preserves executed report cells for a pinned edition, while the per-model dashboards under `docs/models/vgNN` remain the detailed diagnostic record. Full reproduction commands and completion checks are given in Appendix D.
